title: Explaining models
abstract: Ensuring fairness of machine learning systems is a human-in-the-loop process. It relies on developers, users, and the general public to identify fairness problems and make improvements. To facilitate the process we need effective, unbiased, and user-friendly explanations that people can confidently rely on. Towards that end, we conducted an empirical study with four types of programmatically generated explanations to understand how they impact people's fairness judgments of ML systems. With an experiment involving more than 160 Mechanical Turk workers, we show that: 1) Certain explanations are considered inherently less fair, while others can enhance people's confidence in the fairness of the algorithm; 2) Different fairness problems-such as model-wide fairness issues versus case-specific fairness discrepancies-may be more effectively exposed through different styles of explanation; 3) Individual differences, including prior positions and judgment criteria of algorithmic fairness, impact how people react to different styles of explanation. We conclude with a discussion on providing personalized and adaptive explanations to support fairness judgments of ML systems.

claims.text: Predictions made on preprocessed (de-biased) data are rated as fairer than those made on raw data.
Predictions on cases exhibiting disparate impact are rated as less fair than those on non-impacted cases.
Local explanation styles (sensitivity-based and case-based) are more effective than global explanation styles in exposing case-specific fairness discrepancies.
Case-based explanations are rated as generally less fair overall compared to influence-based and demographic-based explanations.
Sensitivity-based explanations significantly lower perceived fairness on disparately impacted cases specifically among individuals who consider using the race feature to be unfair.
An individual's prior trust in machine learning systems positively correlates with their overall perceived fairness ratings of model predictions.
Global explanations enhance perceived model fairness to a greater extent among users who already possess prior trust in machine learning systems.

limitations.text: The study was conducted with crowdworkers rather than judges or domain experts who would be actual users of algorithmic recidivism prediction tools.
Model prediction confidence scores were not presented to participants in order to control for confounding variables.
Prior work examined fairness perceptions using fictional scenarios with explanations not drawn from real ML model outputs or incommensurate data points across conditions.

future_work.text: Providing personalized and adaptive explanations tailored to individual user profiles and prior fairness positions to support fairness judgments.
Developing active-learning paradigms for fairness improvement, where systems query human fairness judgments on predictions and explanations to optimize underlying algorithms based on feedback.
Designing hybrid explanation techniques that combine global overview with local case scrutiny tailored to specific feature space regions and fairness issues.

methodologies.name: Controlled User Experiment on ML Fairness Perception
methodologies.description: An online mixed-design user study with 160 Mechanical Turk workers evaluating fairness judgments across 4 programmatically generated explanation styles, 2 data processing treatments (raw vs. preprocessed), and cases with or without disparate impact.
